confusionCorner.body: When moving a term, use the opposite operation. If you have $ -2x $ on the left, add $ 2x $ to both sides to move it. Don't subtract $ 2x $ – that would make it $ -4x $.

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine two runners starting a race from opposite ends of a track. The equation has variable terms on both sides, just like having runners moving in opposite directions. To find when they meet, you gather all the motion (variable terms) onto one side!

explanation: Some equations have variable terms on both sides of the equals sign.
The goal is still to isolate the variable, but first we must [[imp:collect all variable terms on one side]].
Use inverse operations (addition or subtraction) to move variable terms from one side to the other.

confusionCorner.body: In an equation like $ 2(4x + 2) = 4x - 12(x - 1) $, the right side has both a term $ 4x $ and a distributed $ -12(x - 1) $. Be careful to distribute only the $ -12 $, not the $ 4x $ term.
confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget the Second Parenthesis

discoveryHook.scenario: Equations sometimes hide their variable terms inside parentheses. The Distributive Property is the key to unwrap them. Once revealed, you can gather those terms and solve with ease!

teacherCues: Write '3(3x - 4) = 1/4 (32x + 56)' on the board. Ask: 'What must we do before collecting variable terms?'
Emphasize: 'Always simplify each side – distribute and combine like terms – before moving terms.'

explanation: When parentheses appear, use the [[kw:Distributive Property]] to expand them.
After distributing, [[imp:combine like terms]] on each side.
Then collect variable terms on one side and constants on the other.
Finally, isolate the variable.

notes: Multiply every term inside by the outside number.

examples.prompt: Determine the number of solutions of $ 4(1 - p) = -4p + 4 $.

teacherCues: Write '3(5x + 2) = 15x' on the board. Simplify to '15x + 6 = 15x', then subtract 15x to get '6 = 0'. Ask: 'What does this mean?'
Contrast with '-2(4y + 1) = -8y - 2' which simplifies to '-8y - 2 = -8y - 2' – an identity.

discoveryHook.scenario: Not all equations have a nice single answer. Some are never true, like saying 6 = 0. Others are always true, no matter what x is. These special cases are the 'tricksters' of algebra – recognizing them saves you from endless solving!

confusionCorner.title: False Statement ≠ No Solution
confusionCorner.body: If your work ends with something like $ x = 0 $, that is one solution! Only if the variable disappears entirely and the remaining statement is false (e.g., $ 0 = 5 $) do you have no solution.

questions.prompt: An equation that is true for all values of the variable is called an ___.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: A false statement means no solution.
questions.prompt: When simplifying leads to a false statement like $ 6 = 0 $, the equation has ___ solution.
hints: It's the opposite of infinitely many.

explanation: After simplifying, if the variable terms cancel and you get a false statement (like $ 6 = 0 $), the equation has [[imp:no solution]].
If the variable terms cancel and you get a true statement (like $ -2 = -2 $), the equation is an [[kw:identity]] and has [[imp:infinitely many solutions]].
These are called [[kw:special solutions]] of linear equations.
Always simplify completely before deciding the number of solutions.

notes: If $ b = c $ → infinitely many solutions.

confusionCorner.title: Defining the Variable Correctly
confusionCorner.body: In the boat problem, $ x $ is the speed upstream, not the distance. The distance is found by multiplying speed by time. Always re-read the question to make sure you answer what's asked.

blocks.title: Real-Life Applications

discoveryHook.scenario: From a boat navigating a river with currents to a cheetah chasing an antelope, equations with variables on both sides model situations where two things are in balance – same distance, same total cost, same meeting point. Algebra helps you find the tipping point!

explanation: Many real-life problems involve quantities that are equal under different conditions.
Set up expressions for each quantity, then equate them.
The resulting equation often has variables on both sides.
Solve the equation using the techniques you've learned.
Check that the answer makes sense in the original context.

notes: Use for upstream/downstream or chasing problems.
Set distances equal when the trips cover the same ground.

examples.prompt: A boat travels upstream for 4 hours. The return trip takes 2.8 hours, with speed 3 mph faster downstream. Find the upstream distance.
steps: Let $ x $ = upstream speed. Downstream speed = $ x + 3 $.
Divide: $ x = 7 $ mph. Upstream distance = $ 4 \times 7 = 28 $ miles.
In time $ t $, cheetah runs $ 90t $, antelope runs $ 60t $ plus the 120 ft head start.

visuals.title: The Blueprint for Variables on Both Sides

rows.1: Distribute and combine like terms on each side.
Add/subtract to get all variable terms on one side, constants on the other.
Multiply/divide to solve; identify no solution or identity if applicable.

notes: Check your solution in the original equation.
formulaCard.title: Blueprint Summary

explanation: The [[imp:Simplify → Collect → Isolate]] blueprint breaks down any equation with variables on both sides.
[[imp:Simplify]]: Distribute and combine like terms on each side.
[[imp:Collect]]: Move all variable terms to one side, constants to the other.
[[imp:Isolate]]: Divide to get the variable alone; then check for special solutions.

hints: It involves distributing and combining like terms.
questions.prompt: What is the first phase of the blueprint for variables on both sides?
In the Collect phase, you move all variable terms to one side and all ___ terms to the other.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Move all constant terms to the other side.
hints: They are the terms you add or subtract to isolate the variable.

questions.prompt: Solve $ 4(x - 3) + 2 = 4x - 10 $ using the blueprint. How many solutions?
hints: See if the variable terms cancel and what remains.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Simplify: 4x - 10 = 4x - 10, which is an identity; infinitely many solutions.

confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget the Blueprint Order
confusionCorner.body: Always simplify before collecting. Attempting to move terms before distributing often leads to errors. A clean, simplified equation is much easier to handle.

discoveryHook.scenario: Equations with variables scattered on both sides can look chaotic. The Simplify → Collect → Isolate blueprint brings order. Just follow the phases and watch the solution appear!

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Solving Equations with Variables on Both Sides
teacherCues: Display the three‑phase blueprint: Simplify → Collect → Isolate. Walk through an example, explicitly labeling each phase.
Point out that 'Collect' replaces the 'Understand' phase from earlier blueprints because the main task is collecting variable terms.

presenterNotes: When introducing variables on both sides, use the balance scale analogy and emphasize that we can add or subtract variable terms just like numbers.
For special solutions, let students discover the 'aha' moment when variables cancel. Have them articulate why 6=0 means no solution.
In the boat problem, emphasize unit analysis: miles/hour × hours = miles. Both sides have units of miles, confirming the equation is correctly set up.
